paras: The threatened lynching of William Keys and Joe Tyler took place in Hagerstown, Maryland, in early December 1903, when townspeople openly advocated lynching two Black men accused in a sex scandal involving white girls. A gang of white men organized to tar and feather them, and the two were warned to leave town, but no attack was reported. The case ran in a few white papers in Maryland, West Virginia and New York, which treated it chiefly as a scandal of interracial "depravity".

Amelia Stanhope Little, a 17-year-old white girl, was committed to the Female House of Refuge until the age of 21 by Justice Hoffman after her mother complained that she was incorrigible and "consorted with" William Keys, a Black man employed at a hotel. According to the Catoctin Clarion, Keys admitted intimacy with the girl, who also implicated his younger brother Frank and Joe Tyler, a cabman, who denied the charge.

On the afternoon of 4 December, at the suggestion of State's Attorney Poffenberger, Justice Hoffman held an investigation at which prisoners who said they had heard Little's confession testified. Four Black men were then arrested on charges of enticing white girls under 18, and the Shepherdstown Register named them as Tyler, George Washington Puller, Harry Goins and George Reed, along with two white women. A Hagerstown dispatch to the New York Sun accused Tyler and Mrs. Albert May of arranging meetings between the men and the girls.

Feeling in the town turned against Keys and Tyler, who were warned to leave. Hoffman told Keys that he "would not answer for the conduct of the people," who were openly calling for lynching, and a gang of 15 young white men organized to tar and feather the Black men and "some disreputable white women" involved. William Keys left town before officers could catch him, and his brother Frank went to Baltimore.
No lynching or tar-and-feathering is reported in the coverage, and no report of a trial of the arrested men was found.

The New York Sun carried the first report on 6 December under the headline "For Enticing White Girls," framing the story around the arrests of "Four Negroes" and the excitement of the citizens, without mention of lynching. The Catoctin Clarion of Mechanicstown, Maryland, gave the fullest account of the threats on 10 December, as one item in a column of state news. The same day the Shepherdstown Register in West Virginia called it "a hideous story" that revealed "a fearful state of depravity," described Tyler as "flat-nosed, burly," and noted the "talk of tar and feathers and lynch law" without comment.
The Parsons Advocate reprinted the Register's paragraph on 24 December. No coverage in the Black press was found.

Accounts differ on why the Keys brothers left: the Catoctin Clarion said they were warned to leave amid lynch talk, while the Sun and the Register described them as leaving ahead of arrest, the Sun adding that Frank had gone to Baltimore the week before.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Keys and Joe Tyler
bases: Keys and Tyler were warned to leave town, lynching was openly advocated and a gang was organized to tar and feather them, but no attack is reported (A2, A3); the Keys brothers' departure is described as flight from arrest (A1, A3) rather than a carried-out expulsion.
Three independently worded reports agree on the Hagerstown scandal and arrests (A1, A2, A3), and two of them report the lynching and tar-and-feather talk (A2, A3).

accounts.label: Hagerstown dispatch
accounts.gist: Four Black men were arrested after Justice Hoffman's investigation, charged with enticing white girls under 18; William Keys left before officers could catch him, and the town was 'excited'. It does not mention lynching talk.

accounts.label: Maryland state news column
accounts.gist: Keys and Tyler were warned to leave town; people openly advocated lynching, Hoffman would not answer for them, and a gang of 15 young white men organized to tar and feather the Black men and white women involved.

accounts.label: West Virginia news paragraph
accounts.gist: Lists those arrested, says the Keys brothers 'skipped town' but would probably be brought back, and notes 'talk of tar and feathers and lynch law'.

framing.detail: The Sun's headline 'For Enticing White Girls' framed the case as a criminal charge against 'Four Negroes' and reported the town's excitement without comment on threats.
The Catoctin Clarion reported the lynching advocacy and tar-and-feather gang flatly within a column of state news, calling the white women 'disreputable'.
The Shepherdstown Register called it 'a hideous story' and 'a fearful state of depravity', described Tyler as 'flat-nosed, burly', and mentioned the lynch talk without condemning it.
